reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: Pes cavus is an abnormally high medial longitudinal arch, commonly with hindfoot varus, a plantarflexed first ray, and clawing of the toes (cavovarus foot)
A cavus foot, especially if progressive, asymmetrical, or associated with clawing, should be assumed to have a neurological cause until proven otherwise
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is the classic hereditary neuropathy underlying cavovarus deformity, but other neuromuscular causes and old trauma also occur
The Coleman block test determines whether hindfoot varus is flexible and driven by the plantarflexed first ray, which corrects when the lateral foot is supported, or fixed
The high arch reduces the weight-bearing area, so load concentrates under the metatarsal heads and heel, causing metatarsalgia and painful callosities
Lateral foot overload predisposes to recurrent ankle sprains, peroneal tendon problems, and lateral column stress fractures
Examination must include a full neurological assessment, family history, and gait analysis, with weight-bearing radiographs to quantify the deformity

Management ranges from cushioned, supportive footwear and orthoses with lateral posting and metatarsal support, through physiotherapy, to osteotomy, tendon transfer, and arthrodesis for fixed deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Pes cavus is an elevation of the medial longitudinal arch that usually reflects a muscle imbalance across the foot rather than a primary bony abnormality. In the common cavovarus pattern, relative weakness of the tibialis anterior and peroneus brevis with preserved or overactive peroneus longus and tibialis posterior plantarflexes the first ray and drives the hindfoot into varus, while intrinsic weakness produces clawing of the toes. This imbalance is characteristically caused by hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies, most notably Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, but also by other neuromuscular disorders, spinal pathology, and sequelae of trauma or compartment syndrome. The rigid high arch concentrates load on the heel and metatarsal heads, producing metatarsalgia and callosities, and the varus hindfoot destabilises the ankle, leading to recurrent lateral ankle sprains, peroneal tendon overload, and lateral column stress injuries. Initially flexible, the deformity tends to stiffen and become fixed as it progresses.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and other hereditary neuropathies
Post-traumatic cavus following compartment syndrome or malunion
Spinal dysraphism, tethered cord, or other central neurological causes
Poliomyelitis or other motor neuropathy sequelae
Friedreich's ataxia and related hereditary ataxias
Idiopathic subtle cavus without an identifiable cause
additionalInvestigations: Full neurological examination and family history to seek a hereditary neuropathy
Coleman block test to determine whether hindfoot varus is flexible or fixed
Weight-bearing foot radiographs to quantify the arch and hindfoot alignment
Nerve conduction studies and neurology referral where a neuromuscular cause is suspected
Spinal MRI if a central or cord lesion is considered, particularly in unilateral or rapidly progressive cases
Genetic testing for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease when clinically indicated
Pedobarography to characterise the abnormal loading pattern
redFlags: Progressive, asymmetrical, or unilateral cavus deformity suggesting an active neurological process such as a tethered cord or tumour
New or evolving neurological deficit requiring urgent neurological and spinal evaluation
Sensory loss with plantar ulceration in a neuropathic foot
Recurrent giving way with ankle instability and lateral column stress injury
Rapid deterioration in gait or balance indicating a progressive neuromuscular disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is closely tied to the underlying cause. Idiopathic or mild cavus may remain stable and manageable with orthoses, but neuropathic cavovarus deformity, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, tends to be progressive and to recur even after surgery because the causative imbalance persists. Combined bony realignment and tendon transfers can restore a plantigrade, stable foot, but long-term orthotic support and monitoring are usually required.
pitfalls: Assuming a cavus foot is idiopathic and failing to search for an underlying neurological cause
Not performing the Coleman block test, so that a flexible hindfoot is treated as if fixed
Correcting bony deformity without addressing the tendon imbalance, leading to recurrence
Overlooking spinal pathology in unilateral or rapidly progressive deformity
Neglecting ankle instability and lateral overload that accompany the varus hindfoot
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
